DLG Republic of the Philippines DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR AND LOCAL GOVERNMENT Francisco Gold Condominium II EDSA Cor. Mapagmahal St., Diliman Quezon City LEGAL SERVICE Legal Opinion No. 33 s. 2011 JUL 0 5 2011 ATTY. GEORGE A. ELIAS Proprietor 09 Gen.Luna St. Tuktukan Taguig City Dear Atty. Elias: We refer to your letter on the issue of the revocation of business permit issued by the Mayor of the City of Taguig, According to you, a revocation letter dated 27 June 2011 was issued by Atty. Fanela Joy B. Panga, Officer-in-Charge of Business Permits and Licensing Office (BPLO), advising you of the revocation of your business permit for giving false statement in his application, a violation of the conditions of the permit issued to you. You further alleged that your rights to due process were violated when BPLO-OIC Atty. Panga revoked the business permit without affording you an opportunity to rectify any shortcoming or defects within a reasonable period of time. In view of the foregoing, you requested for legal opinion on the six (6) questions or issues you raised: 1. 2. 3. 4. 5. 6. Whether or not an Officer-in-Charge of the BPLO is authorized to cause the revocation of a business permit issued by the mayor? Is there legal basis for the revocation of our business permit based allegedly for (sic) "gross misinformation" on a document (tax declaration) not required by the BPLO in its checklist of requirements for issuance of business permit? Could "gross misinformation" be the basis for revocation when we had sought the reclassification of a property based on its actual use? Considering that an ordinance is required for reclassification of parcel of land from residential to commercial, would a zoning ordinance which classified the land as GENERAL RESIDENTIAL ZONE 1, which allows commercial use thereof, plus the passage of a Sanggunian resolution suffice for the assessor to reclassify the land? Can the BPLO unilaterally adjudicate on the vafidity of a resotution reclassifying a parcel of land without recourse to the proper courts? Should the BPLO insist on the revocation of the permit, what are the remedies available to us?

As to Your First, Second and Third Queries: cause the A BPLO Head or an Officer-in-Charge (OIC), by himself, may not revocation of the business permit issued by the Office of the Mayor. BPLO may recommend the revocation of a business permit after due process is accorded to the holder of the permit or license. As permits and licenses are issued for regulatory purposes and under certain conditions upon which they are issued pursuant to a law or ordinance, the entitlement thereof is not a matter of right but a privilege, and neither is it a property. A license or a permit is not a contract between the sovereignty and the licensee or permitee, and is not a property in the constitutional sense, as to which the constitutional proscription against impairment of the obligation of contracts may extend. A license is rather in the nature of a special privilege, of a permission or authority to do what is within its terms. It is not in any way vested, permanent or absolute, (Acebedo Optica/ Company Inc. vs Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 100152, 31 March 2000) Hypothetically, a gross misinformation may be a ground for revocation of the business permit and license if the act constitutes any violation of the conditions upon which said permit or license are issued, particularly if the misinformation pertains to the data supplied in the application for permit and license. In relation to your case, OIC Atty. Panga alleged that the gross misinformation that "as lessor of commercia/ spaces, the lot is situated in a pertained to your commercia/ area", predicated on Resolution No. 27, Series of 2011. Atty. Panga claim was "misleading, the purported legal basis for your asserted that erroneous, and without merit" because per zoning certification, the iot is classified as General Residential Development Zone 1. Further, Atty. Panga emphasized that "reclassification of lands by /oca/ legislative councils are made through an ordinance and not a mere resolution". Under the circumstances, we shall defer passing upon the validity nor sufficiency of the claims of either party considering the opposing views respectively taken, and are in the nature of evidentiary claims that require evaluation, assessment and appreciation thereof. As to Your Fourth Query: Section 20 of RA 7160 provides for the reclassification of land which may be validly made through an ordinance passed by the sanggunian concerned after the conduct of public hearing held for that purpose. The local government units shall, in conformity with existing laws, continue to prepare their respective comprehensive land use plans enacted through zoning ordinances which shall be the primary and dominant bases for the future use of land resources. (Section 20 [c], RA 7160)

Fina//y, As to Your Fifth and Sixth Query: A BPLO cannot unilaterally adjudicate on the validity of a resolution. An ordinance or resolution duly enacted and passed by the local sanggunian is presumed valid. The adjudication on whether an ordinance or resolution is valid or not rests on the sound wisdom of the judicial court. Until the declaration of nullity, an assailed ordinance or resolution is presumed consistent with the law and therefore valid (Section 56 [d]/ RA 7160) There is no basis for this Office to render any opinion on the claim by BPLO on the alleged "dubious promulgation of Resolution No. 27, Series of 2011". Neither does this Office have any document that refers to the said resolution . On the matter on which proper remedy should be taken, we cite the following cases: "The power of the xxx mayor to issue license and permits is circumscribed, is a manifestation of the delegated police power of a municipal corporation. Necessarily, the exercise thereof cannot be deemed ministerial. As to the question of whether the power is validly exercised, the matter is within the province of a writ of certiorari, but certainly, not of mandamus. " (Arrastre vs Villaflor) "The regulatory powers granted to municipal corporations must always be exercised in accordance with law, with utmost observance of the rights of the people to due process and equal protection of the law. Such power cannot be exercised whimsically, arbitrarily or despotically, In the instant case, we find that Lim's exercise of this power violated Bistro's property rights that are protected under the due process clause of the Constitution. " (Lim and Garayblas vs Court of Appeals, G.R. No. 111397, 12 August 2002) We hope to have sufficiently addressed your concerns. Very truly yours, ATTY. JESUS DIRECTOR 111 .
